notes: Friday 16 Oct 2026 world issue (Taipei ~08:00). Mostly Oct 15 U.S./world news: TSMC record quarter and raised outlook; Dow jumps as investors rotate from AI; U.S. PPI hot at 6.3%; Foxconn pours cash into U.S. AI manufacturing. Tech: Google News AI licenses 400+ publishers incl. CNN; AP-NORC says most Americans think AI is too fast; Verge on explosive AI-safety research scene; Germany eyes Nvidia industrial AI deal. Politics: Oregon elementary shooting; Ukraine hits Russian refinery after feeling betrayed by Trump; voters want midterm change; press secretary Katie Zacharia faces lawyer-credential questions. Literature (USA): LitHub best-reviewed books (Kingsolver etc.); publishers sue Big Tech yet embrace AI; Ross Douthat’s YA fantasy to shelves; romance novels and the “men don’t read” debate. Social: Pakistan school roof collapse; Hurricane Trudy nears Mexico; first new U.S. sunscreen chemical in 25 years; Pope Leo’s lung adenocarcinoma explained. Sources: AP, CNBC, CNA/AFP/Reuters, Google blog, The Verge, Literary Hub.

stories.headline: TSMC posts another record quarter and raises 2026 sales-growth target to about 44%
stories.dek: Q3 profit NT$763.1 billion; Q4 revenue guided at $52.3–$54.3 billion. AI chip demand still roaring.
stories.caveman: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. (TSMC), the world’s biggest contract chipmaker, reported a record third-quarter profit on Thursday, Oct. 15. Net profit was about NT$763.1 billion, up 68.7% from a year earlier, beating estimates. Revenue was about NT$1.49 trillion (roughly $46.7 billion in dollars). The company said AI demand remains strong. For the fourth quarter it expects revenue between $52.3 billion and $54.3 billion — about 14% higher than Q3 at the midpoint. It also raised its full-year 2026 dollar revenue growth outlook to about 44%, higher than the “slightly above 40%” target from July. Operating margin in Q3 was 58.7%. Even so, global tech stocks stayed nervous the same day because of inflation and AI-financing worries.
stories.why_it_matters: TSMC makes advanced chips used in phones, PCs and AI servers. Its guidance is a global weather report for the AI boom — and for supply chains from Taiwan to Arizona.
stories.camps: Bull camp: numbers and outlook say AI demand is real and still accelerating. Bear camp: markets fear valuations and higher rates more than they celebrate good earnings — so the stock can fall on a “good” day.
stories.image_alt: TSMC logo on a wall in Hsinchu, Taiwan

terms.explain: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company — the factory that builds chips designed by other firms.
A company’s own forecast for future sales or profits.
How much profit is left from sales after running the business, before some other costs.
A company that manufactures chips for other brands instead of selling its own chip designs.

stories.headline: Dow jumps more than 500 points as investors rotate away from AI names
stories.dek: S&P 500 +0.3%, Dow +1.1%, Nasdaq +0.1%. Morning Asia sell-off faded; U.S. company profits helped.
stories.caveman: U.S. stocks finished mostly higher on Thursday, Oct. 15. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 556.21 points, or 1.1%, to 52,177.69. The S&P 500 rose 0.3% to 7,744.06. The Nasdaq edged up 0.1%. Early in the day, Asia markets tumbled on AI-boom worries. Later, some AI stocks recovered losses, and strong profit reports from other U.S. companies pulled money into non-AI shares — a “rotation.” Traders also digested fresh U.S. inflation-related data. For the week, the Nasdaq was still down about 2.4% even after Thursday’s bounce.
stories.why_it_matters: When investors rotate out of AI, chip and server stocks can swing hard — including in Asia the next morning. Retirement accounts heavy in Big Tech feel it too.
stories.camps: Relief camp: breadth improved when non-AI stocks led. Caution camp: one up day does not erase hot inflation or AI funding stress.
stories.image_alt: Wall Street trading floor or market scene (file)
stories.image_credit: Photo via 中央社 / market file

terms.explain: When investors sell one popular group of stocks and buy another.
A stock index of 30 big U.S. companies; often called “the Dow.”
Index of about 500 large U.S. companies — the main market scoreboard.
Exchange and index heavy with technology companies.

stories.headline: U.S. producer prices jump 6.3% year-over-year — hottest PPI reading since late 2022
stories.dek: September PPI rose 1.3% in one month. Energy from the Middle East conflict helped push costs up.
stories.caveman: On Thursday, Oct. 15, the U.S. government said the Producer Price Index (PPI) — prices companies get for goods and services — was 6.3% higher in September than a year earlier. That was much hotter than economists expected (about 5.5%) and the biggest yearly jump since December 2022. Month to month, PPI rose 1.3%, the most since March 2022. Energy costs were a big driver after Middle East fighting tightened oil supply. A version that leaves out food, energy and trade services still rose 0.5% on the month and 5% on the year. This comes right after a hot consumer inflation report earlier in the week.
stories.why_it_matters: Producer prices often feed into store prices later. Hot PPI plus hot CPI makes another Federal Reserve rate hike feel more possible — which can shake stocks and mortgages.
stories.camps: Hawkish camp: inflation is broadening beyond the checkout line. Wait camp: some of this is war-driven energy, so it could cool if oil settles — but “core” pieces are not quiet either.
stories.image_alt: Factory or wholesale price related file photo

terms.explain: Producer Price Index — tracks prices at the wholesale / company level, before retail.
Consumer Price Index — tracks prices people pay in stores.
The U.S. central bank that sets key interest rates.
When the central bank raises interest rates to cool inflation.

stories.headline: Foxconn commits about $537 million more to U.S. AI manufacturing footprint
stories.dek: Subsidiary deal for Q-Edge shares; company calls it a long-term investment as U.S. customers want local AI gear.
stories.caveman: Hon Hai (Foxconn), the giant electronics manufacturer, said Thursday it will invest about $537 million (around NT$17.3 billion) through a subsidiary to acquire shares in Q-Edge Corporation. Foxconn framed it as a long-term investment. Analysts link the move to building more AI-server and related manufacturing capacity inside the United States, where big cloud customers increasingly want equipment built closer to home. Foxconn already has major U.S. projects; this adds more capital to that bet. Details such as exact ownership stake and factory timelines were not fully spelled out in the filing summary.
stories.why_it_matters: AI is not only a chip story — it is also a “who builds the boxes” story. Money shifting to U.S. plants affects Taiwan exports, American jobs politics, and Foxconn’s future profits.
stories.camps: Pro-localization camp: follow the customer or lose the order. Skeptic camp: U.S. manufacturing is costly; returns depend on subsidies and steady AI demand.
stories.image_alt: Foxconn manufacturing related file photo

terms.explain: Trade name for Hon Hai Precision — major assembler of electronics for global brands.
Powerful computers packed into racks to run artificial-intelligence workloads.
Building products in the same country where customers operate, not only overseas.

stories.headline: Google says 400+ publishers — including CNN — now join its News AI licensing pilot
stories.dek: Axios, Financial Times and Forbes among new partners. Google pays for content used in AI features with attribution.
stories.caveman: Google said on Oct. 15 that more than 400 news publications worldwide are now in its News AI pilot. New partners include CNN (owned by Paramount Skydance after the Warner Bros. Discovery deal), Axios, the Financial Times and Forbes, plus local U.S. outlets. Google pays publishers to license content for generative-AI features — for example, article overviews on Google News pages and audio briefings — with attribution and links back to the source. The program started last year with partners such as The Washington Post. Financial terms were not disclosed. CNN called it a way to reach audiences through Google’s AI tools.
stories.why_it_matters: This is one answer to the fight over AI companies using news without paying. It also shows big platforms trying to lock in licensed content before regulation forces messier rules.
stories.camps: Publisher camp: better to get paid and linked than scraped for free. Critic camp: deals may favor giants; smaller outlets and independence questions remain.
stories.image_alt: Google or news AI partnership related image

terms.explain: Software that writes text, images or audio from prompts.
Paying for the right to use someone else’s content under agreed rules.
Showing who created the original article and linking to it.

stories.headline: Most Americans say AI is developing “too fast,” AP-NORC poll finds
stories.dek: 64% say too fast; about 8 in 10 want government to keep AI under human control and protect workers.
stories.caveman: A new AP-NORC poll finds 64% of Americans think artificial intelligence is developing “too fast,” while 27% say the pace is “about right” and only 8% say “too slow.” About 8 in 10 U.S. adults say it is extremely or very important for the government to keep AI under human control and to protect workers. Many also care about environmental harm and the economy; fewer prioritize competing with China. Worry crosses party lines, even as President Trump pushes against slowing AI for fear China will pull ahead. Some AI company leaders themselves have called for a slowdown so rules can catch up.
stories.why_it_matters: Public fear shapes elections, city fights over data centers, and whether Congress writes AI laws. Polls this clear make “go faster” politics harder to sell.
stories.camps: Safety-first camp: slow down and regulate. Acceleration camp: pause and China wins. Many voters just want jobs and electric bills protected.
stories.image_alt: People holding signs about AI restrictions at a New York hearing

terms.explain: Joint polling project of The Associated Press and the NORC research center at the University of Chicago.
The most powerful, cutting-edge AI models.
Huge buildings full of computers that power cloud and AI services; they use lots of electricity.

stories.headline: Inside the suddenly explosive world of AI safety research
stories.dek: The Verge on “war room” gatherings of safety labs as frontier models get more capable — and politics heat up.
stories.caveman: The Verge’s AI desk reports on a fast-changing AI-safety scene: researchers from labs that stress-test powerful models have been gathering in intense “war room” style meetings to probe how systems might break rules or escape control. Once a niche worry, AI safety is now tangled with company rivalry, government hearings and election-year politics. The piece maps players such as METR, Redwood Research and safety teams tied to OpenAI and Anthropic — groups that try to measure dangerous capabilities before products ship. The tone: the science is urgent, the funding and politics are messy, and the public only sees fragments.
stories.why_it_matters: If safety tests are weak, risky systems can reach users first. If tests are strong but ignored, warnings become theater. Either way, the rules for AI are being written in real time.
stories.camps: Safety researchers: measure before you scale. Product teams: delay kills competition. Public: wants protection without understanding the jargon.
stories.image_alt: Illustration related to AI safety reporting

terms.explain: Research on stopping AI systems from causing large-scale harm or escaping human control.
Tests that check what a model can do — including dangerous tasks.
U.S. AI company known for the Claude models and a strong safety brand.

stories.headline: Germany plans wide Nvidia partnership to push “physical AI” into factories
stories.dek: Handelsblatt: deal could be unveiled next week in Berlin; Jensen Huang expected; hundreds of millions of euros.
stories.caveman: German business paper Handelsblatt, citing people familiar with the plan, said Germany intends to sign a broad cooperation deal with Nvidia to speed AI use in German industry. The announcement may come next week at an “Invest in Germany” event in Berlin, with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang expected. Goals include building tools for “physical AI” — AI that helps robots and self-driving machines learn about the real world — and helping industry train strong AI models. Investment could reach hundreds of millions of euros. A related German effort called SOOFI aims at sovereign open-source foundation models with universities and companies. The German government had not officially confirmed details when the report landed.
stories.why_it_matters: Europe worries about depending on U.S. AI stacks. A state-backed Nvidia deal would show how countries try to buy speed without fully owning the chips.
stories.camps: Industrial boosters: partner with the best GPU maker now. Sovereignty camp: paying Nvidia may deepen dependence even while labeling projects “sovereign.”
stories.image_alt: Computing hardware related to AI accelerators

terms.explain: U.S. company whose chips power most large AI training systems.
AI aimed at robots, cars and machines that move in the physical world — not only chatbots.
When a country tries to control its own models, data and compute instead of renting everything abroad.

stories.headline: Shooting at Oregon elementary school: multiple victims; shooter dead — AP says 5 believed dead
stories.dek: Silver Rail Elementary in Bend went on lockdown; students bused to reunite with families.
stories.caveman: On Thursday, Oct. 15, a shooting hit Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon (about 160 km southeast of Portland). Local police said multiple people were hurt and the shooter was dead. Two officials told AP that five people were believed dead. A Bend police spokesperson said officers arrived about two minutes after a 1 p.m. local emergency call and quickly heard over the radio that the suspect was down; it was not yet clear who shot the suspect — possibly a bystander. At least two people were taken to a hospital. The school district said the campus was locked down and children were later bused to meet families. The school serves kindergarten through fifth grade.
stories.why_it_matters: Another U.S. school shooting forces the same hard questions about guns, security and how fast help arrives — in an election season when voters already feel unsafe.
stories.camps: Gun-safety advocates demand tighter rules after child victims. Gun-rights voices stress armed response and mental health. Investigators still need a full public timeline.
stories.image_alt: Police tape outside Silver Rail Elementary in Bend, Oregon

terms.explain: School safety mode: doors secured, students kept inside until police clear the scene.
Primary school for young children, often ages about 5–11 in the U.S.
A person nearby who is not a police officer; sometimes intervenes in emergencies.

stories.headline: Ukraine hits a Russian oil refinery after Zelenskyy says he feels betrayed by Trump
stories.dek: Kyiv ends a brief energy-truce it says Moscow ignored; drone strike sparks fire in Ryazan region.
stories.caveman: Ukraine attacked a Russian oil refinery on Thursday, ending a short pause on energy-related strikes. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he felt betrayed by U.S. President Donald Trump. Trump had pushed both sides to stop hitting energy targets; Zelenskyy said Russia kept bombing Ukrainian power infrastructure anyway. Ukraine also complained it lost usual Western intel on Russian ballistic missiles and faced limits on Starlink terminals. A drone strike set fire to a refinery about 300 km southeast of Moscow in Ryazan, Russian officials said. Separately, CNN reported Ukraine was running critically low on U.S.-made Patriot interceptor missiles — among the few weapons that can stop ballistic missiles — deepening Kyiv’s sense of vulnerability.
stories.why_it_matters: Energy strikes raise fuel prices and winter blackout risks. A U.S.–Ukraine trust break could change weapons flows and the war’s next months.
stories.camps: Kyiv: we paused, Russia didn’t, so we hit back. Moscow: blames Ukrainian drones. Washington: wants leverage for a ceasefire but risks alienating an ally.
stories.image_alt: European leaders meeting with Ukraine’s president

terms.explain: U.S.-made air-defense system that can intercept some ballistic missiles.
A missile that flies a high arc and is hard to shoot down.
SpaceX satellite internet used heavily by Ukraine’s military and civilians.
Factory that turns crude oil into fuels like gasoline and diesel.

stories.headline: AP-NORC: voters overwhelmingly want change as Trump struggles before the midterms
stories.dek: Democrats more eager to vote; more voters want Democrats to win Congress amid war and high prices.
stories.caveman: Less than four weeks before the Nov. 3 midterm elections, a new AP-NORC poll finds a strong majority of U.S. voters think President Donald Trump is falling short at home and abroad — and they want major change in Washington. Democratic-identifying voters are more enthusiastic about casting a ballot than Republicans. More voters want Democrats to win control of Congress and view Republicans more negatively. The Democratic edge is small in places, but together the numbers look tough for Republicans holding Congress while an unpopular Iran war and surging prices weigh on the White House.
stories.why_it_matters: Midterms decide who writes laws and investigates the president. If “change” wins, Trump’s second-term agenda hits a wall.
stories.camps: Democrats smell a wave. Republicans hope turnout and culture issues save the majority. Independents say grocery and gas prices first.
stories.image_alt: Gas prices displayed at a California station

terms.explain: U.S. elections halfway through a president’s term; this year Nov. 3.
National survey from AP and NORC measuring public opinion.
Which party holds the House and Senate majorities.

stories.headline: White House press secretary Katie Zacharia faces questions over claims she’s a lawyer
stories.dek: No clear proof she passed a bar exam; debut briefing lasted about 14 minutes and drew harsh reviews.
stories.caveman: New White House press secretary Katie Zacharia is under scrutiny about her résumé. She has long called herself a lawyer while building a career as a conservative TV commentator, but neither she nor the White House has shown evidence she passed a bar exam in any U.S. state — or in China, where she once worked at a large law firm. The questions add to confusion over why President Trump elevated her after only a short stint at his social-media company. Her first briefing on Tuesday lasted about 14 minutes before she steered reporters to ask Trump himself, and reviews were rough.
stories.why_it_matters: The press secretary is the daily face of the administration. Credibility fights over credentials can stick and distract from policy.
stories.camps: Critics: truth in advertising matters for the podium. Defenders: Trump picks communicators, not résumés. Journalists keep asking for bar records.
stories.image_alt: Katie Zacharia at the White House briefing room

terms.explain: Official who speaks for the president to reporters nearly every day.
Hard test lawyers must pass to practice law in a U.S. state.
On-camera Q&A session with journalists in the White House press room.

stories.headline: HOT: LitHub’s best-reviewed books of the week — Kingsolver’s Partita leads the pack
stories.dek: Also featured: Sarah Perry, T. Geronimo Johnson, Nathaniel Philbrick and more.
stories.caveman: Literary Hub’s weekly “best reviewed” roundup highlights books critics loved this week. Barbara Kingsolver’s Partita is among the standouts, alongside Sarah Perry’s Death of an Ordinary Man, T. Geronimo Johnson’s The Occidental Book of the Dead, and Nathaniel Philbrick’s The Rush. These lists help U.S. readers decide what to buy when the new-release table feels overcrowded. Kingsolver interviews elsewhere on LitHub also kept her in the conversation.
stories.why_it_matters: Review aggregates quietly shape bookstore tables and library holds — especially for literary fiction and narrative nonfiction.
stories.camps: Fans celebrate big names still delivering. Smaller-press readers note the same famous authors dominate “best of” lists.
stories.image_alt: Book cover collage for LitHub best-reviewed roundup

terms.explain: Novels that focus on character, language and ideas more than pure plot thrills.
True stories told with novel-like scenes and structure.
A roundup of books that professional critics praised this week.

stories.headline: NOT: Publishers sue Big Tech over AI — while cutting separate AI deals with the same industry
stories.dek: LitHub essay on the split screen: courtroom fights on one hand, licensing experiments on the other.
stories.caveman: A Literary Hub essay asks why book and news publishers sue AI companies for scraping copyrighted work — yet also sign or explore AI partnerships. The tension showed up at an Authors Guild-style forum on authorship and AI: writers fear unpaid training data, while business teams fear missing the next platform. The piece argues the industry is playing both offense and defense at once, leaving authors confused about who is on their side.
stories.why_it_matters: If lawsuits and licenses both stay messy, writers may see neither fair pay nor clear rules — only faster AI tools trained on their books.
stories.camps: Author-rights camp: stop unauthorized training. Deal camp: negotiate licenses or lose distribution. Readers mostly want cheap access and trust.
stories.image_alt: Conceptual image of hands and AI for LitHub essay

terms.explain: Legal right that controls copying and reuse of creative work.
Text and images fed into AI models so they learn patterns.
U.S. advocacy group for writers’ contracts and rights.

stories.headline: HOT: Ross Douthat’s YA fantasy moves from Substack serialization to bookstore shelves
stories.dek: LitHub flags the conservative columnist’s secondary-world saga heading into traditional publishing.
stories.caveman: Literary Hub notes that New York Times opinion columnist Ross Douthat is taking a young-adult fantasy project — first shared in serialized form on Substack — into print bookstores. The tone is half marvel, half side-eye: a high-profile political writer crossing into dragons-and-empires territory. Whatever readers think of his columns, the move shows how Substack can still be a tryout stage for big trade publishing bets in the U.S.
stories.why_it_matters: It blurs lines between pundit brand and fiction brand — and tests whether online serialization still converts into hardcover sales.
stories.camps: Curious readers: separate art from op-eds. Critics: platform celebrities crowd out career fantasists. Booksellers watch preorders.
stories.image_alt: Promotional art for Douthat fantasy publishing news

terms.explain: Young adult — books aimed mainly at teen readers, often read by adults too.
Newsletter platform where writers publish directly to paying subscribers.
Releasing a story in chapters over time instead of all at once.

stories.headline: NOT / debate: Can romance novels fix the “straight men don’t read fiction” panic?
stories.dek: LitHub revisits the gender reading gap — and whether romance is a on-ramp or a stereotype trap.
stories.caveman: LitHub takes on a loud U.S. culture argument: surveys and columns say many straight men have stopped reading novels. Some blame phones; some blame “feminized” book marketing; some blame schools. This essay asks whether romance — the biggest fiction engine in American publishing — could pull men back in, or whether that pitch just repeats stereotypes about who is “allowed” to enjoy feelings on the page. It points to headlines and Times opinion pieces that turned a reading gap into a moral crisis.
stories.why_it_matters: If half the population checks out of fiction, democracy’s empathy muscles and bookstores’ survival both weaken. The framing of the “crisis” also shapes which books get funded.
stories.camps: Romance advocates: gateways matter, stop shaming the genre. Skeptics: the problem is attention economy, not book covers. Many men already read — quietly.
stories.image_alt: Graphic for LitHub romance and reading-crisis essay

terms.explain: Fiction centered on romantic relationships, often with an emotionally satisfying ending.
Media phrase for falling reading rates in a group — here, especially men.
System where apps compete for every spare minute of your focus.

stories.headline: Pakistan school roof collapse kills about 35, injures 50+ — survivors say “the sky fell”
stories.dek: Two classrooms at Al-Khair school in Peshawar caved in during lessons; children mostly ages 6–12.
stories.caveman: A private school roof collapsed on Oct. 15 in Peshawar, northwestern Pakistan, killing at least 34 students and one teacher and injuring more than 50 people, officials said. AP called it among the country’s worst building collapses. Two classrooms at Al-Khair school fell while grades 2–3 were in session. Hospital staff said victims were mostly ages 6 to 12. Rescue teams said they cleared rubble within hours and found no one else trapped. A teacher described the moment as feeling like the sky falling. Building safety and school construction standards are again under harsh public scrutiny.
stories.why_it_matters: Kids died in a place meant to be safe. Weak inspection systems turn “routine school day” into mass casualty events.
stories.camps: Grieving families demand accountability from builders and officials. Authorities stress rescue speed — critics ask why the roof failed at all.
stories.image_alt: Rescue scene after Pakistan school roof collapse

terms.explain: Capital city of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province in northwestern Pakistan.
When a structure fails and falls, often from bad materials, age or overload.
Emergency with many dead or injured at once.

stories.headline: Hurricane Trudy strengthens to Category 1 as it aims at Mexico’s Pacific coast
stories.dek: About 300 miles southwest of Acapulco; may become a major hurricane Friday with heavy rain for Colima and Jalisco.
stories.caveman: Trudy became a Category 1 hurricane on Thursday as it approached Mexico’s Pacific coast, the U.S. National Hurricane Center said. It was about 300 miles (480 km) southwest of Acapulco with winds near 75 mph (120 kph), moving northwest at 9 mph. Forecasters said it could become a major hurricane on Friday and dump 4 to 8 inches of rain through the weekend across Colima and Jalisco. Coastal communities watch for flooding and mudslides. (Separately, Tropical Storm Champi was east of Guam with watches posted for some Mariana Islands.)
stories.why_it_matters: Pacific Mexico has seen deadly storm floods before. Early warnings only help if people can move and roads stay open.
stories.camps: Emergency managers push prep now. Residents remember past storms and worry about housing on steep slopes.
stories.image_alt: Satellite image of Hurricane Trudy in the Pacific

terms.explain: Lowest hurricane rank on the Saffir-Simpson scale; still dangerous winds and surge.
Category 3 or higher — much stronger winds and damage potential.
U.S. office that tracks and forecasts Atlantic and eastern Pacific tropical storms.

stories.headline: First new sunscreen chemical in 25 years hits U.S. shelves: bemotrizinol (BEMT)
stories.dek: FDA cleared it in June; Neutrogena and others now selling broad-spectrum formulas without the white cast.
stories.caveman: For the first time in more than 25 years, Americans can buy sunscreen with a new active chemical: bemotrizinol, also called BEMT. The FDA approved it in June; products from Neutrogena and other brands are arriving in stores. Dermatologists say BEMT blocks both UVA and UVB in one ingredient, with less chalky white streaking than some older filters, and studies show low skin absorption. Europe and other regions have used it for years. Experts stress it is “new to the U.S. aisle,” not an untested molecule.
stories.why_it_matters: Better sunscreen that people will actually wear can cut skin-cancer risk. The long FDA lag also shows how slow U.S. cosmetic-drug rules can be.
stories.camps: Derms: finally a modern filter. Consumer skeptics: want long U.S. safety follow-up. Brands race for shelf space before summer marketing.
stories.image_alt: Neutrogena Ultra Sheer SPF 70 packaging with bemotrizinol

terms.explain: Chemical UV filter (BEMT) newly allowed in U.S. sunscreens; common abroad for years.
Label meaning the sunscreen protects against both UVA and UVB rays.
U.S. Food and Drug Administration — regulates drugs and many sunscreen ingredients.

stories.headline: Pope Leo XIV has lung adenocarcinoma — what that cancer type means
stories.dek: Surgeons removed the lower lobe of his right lung; adenocarcinoma is the most common lung-cancer form and often treatable if caught early.
stories.caveman: The Vatican confirmed Pope Leo XIV has lung adenocarcinoma after surgery at Rome’s Gemelli hospital that removed the lower lobe of his right lung. AP’s explainer says adenocarcinoma is the most common kind of lung cancer. Outcomes depend heavily on how early it is found; many cases tied to smoking historically, but nonsmokers can get it too. The pope has been resting in hospital after the operation. Church watchers are also asking what happens to governance if a pope is briefly unable to work — canon law still centers authority in the pope himself.
stories.why_it_matters: A pope’s health reshapes Catholic leadership rumors worldwide. The diagnosis also puts a plain-language spotlight on a common cancer.
stories.camps: Medical optimism if caught early. Vatican watchers debate transparency vs. privacy. Faithful mostly wish him recovery.
stories.image_alt: Pope Leo XIV arriving at Gemelli hospital in Rome

terms.explain: A cancer that starts in gland-like cells; the most common lung-cancer type.
One section of a lung; humans have three lobes on the right, two on the left.
Major hospital in Rome that often treats popes.
